What is GitHub Copilot?

The most widely distributed AI coding assistant. Plugs into 40+ IDEs as an extension, offering inline completions, chat, multi-file agent mode and deep GitHub-native workflows including PR review and issue-to-code.

Best for

Teams already on GitHub who want AI in their existing editor without switching tools.

Main features

  • Inline code completions and Next Edit Suggestions (unmetered on every plan)
  • Copilot Chat in IDE and on github.com
  • Agent mode for multi-file changes
  • Copilot code review on pull requests
  • Copilot Workspace
  • coding agent that opens PRs from issues
  • model choice across Claude, GPT and Gemini families
  • custom instructions and prompt files
  • enterprise policy controls and audit logs.

Practical use cases

  • Autocompleting boilerplate and tests
  • explaining unfamiliar code
  • multi-file refactors via agent mode
  • automated first-pass PR review
  • turning an issue into a draft pull request
  • onboarding onto a large codebase.

Who is it for?

  • Individual developers, engineering teams, and enterprises standardised on GitHub.

Pricing, free access & limits

Hybrid - per-seat subscription plus usage-based GitHub AI Credits (since 1 June 2026)

Plans described in the source

Free $0 with a monthly allowance of completions and chat. Pro $10/user/mo. Pro+ $39/user/mo. Business $19/user/mo. Enterprise $39/user/mo. As of 1 June 2026 all plans moved to usage-based billing via GitHub AI Credits, calculated on token consumption (input, output, cached); code completions and Next Edit Suggestions remain unmetered on every plan. Free for verified students, teachers and maintainers of popular open-source projects.

Free plan

Yes - a free tier with a capped monthly allowance of completions and chat messages.

Free trial

Yes - 30-day free trial on Pro; free permanently for verified students, teachers and popular OSS maintainers.

Usage limits to consider

Premium model requests and agent runs draw on a monthly GitHub AI Credit allowance that varies by tier; exceeding it incurs overage or throttling. Completions and Next Edit Suggestions are explicitly unmetered.

Strengths & tradeoffs

These points summarize the supplied research, rather than hands-on test results.

Strengths noted in the source

  • Lowest entry price at $10 and a real free tier
  • works in your existing editor so there is no migration
  • unmetered completions mean everyday autocomplete never costs extra
  • unmatched GitHub-native workflows (PR review, issue-to-PR)
  • strongest enterprise governance and audit in the category.

Limitations to consider

  • The agent is less capable than Cursor's or Claude Code's on large multi-file tasks
  • the June 2026 shift to credit billing makes costs less predictable for heavy users
  • premium model access is now metered
  • chat context handling is weaker than AI-native editors.

Platforms, languages & integrations

Platforms

  • VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, Xcode, Eclipse, Zed, github.com, GitHub Mobile, GitHub CLI (40+ surfaces)

Languages

  • All mainstream programming languages; strongest on Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C#, Go

API access

Indirect - GitHub Models API and Copilot Extensions SDK

Integrations and exports

  • GitHub end-to-end (issues, PRs, Actions, Codespaces), Azure DevOps, MCP servers, Copilot Extensions from third parties

Evaluation notes

The 2026 billing change is the key planning item - budget for credit consumption on top of seats if your team leans on agent mode and premium models. For pure autocomplete, cost is still effectively the seat price.
